title: Extinction law and stellar mass in the Nuclear Bulge from kinematically-selected red clump stars
comment: 17 pages, 11 figures, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: The Nuclear Bulge of the Milky Way harbors stellar populations that provide crucial insights into galaxy formation processes and serve as a nearby analog for understanding bulge formation in external galaxies. However, detailed studies of this region are severely hampered by extreme and highly variable interstellar extinction, which obscures the intrinsic stellar properties and impedes accurate stellar mass determinations. Our goal is to measure the extinction law towards the Nuclear Bulge and to estimate its stellar density. We developed a method to determine the extinction law towards the Nuclear Bulge by kinematically selecting red clump stars belonging to this region. We created a high-spatial resolution reddening map, and computed stellar mass with completeness-corrected red clump star counts, scaled from empirical measurements. We find a total-to-selective extinction ratio of $\mathrm{A_K/{E_{H-K}} = 1.259 \pm 0.074}$, and an extinction ratio of $\mathrm{A_H/A_K = 1.794 \pm 0.046}$, which are consistent with previous works. The high-spatial resolution reddening map shows clear filamentary structures, and a gradient in the extinction over the giant molecular cloud G0.253+0.016 (i.e., the Brick). From the star counts, we measured a stellar mass of $\mathrm{12.2~\pm2.6\times10^8~M_{\odot}}$ for the Nuclear Bulge, in agreement with other mass estimates.

AI.tldr: This paper measures the extinction law and stellar mass of the Milky Way's Nuclear Bulge using kinematically selected red clump stars, finding extinction ratios consistent with prior work and a stellar mass of ~1.22×10⁹ M☉.
AI.motivation: The Nuclear Bulge holds key insights into galaxy formation, but its study is hampered by extreme and highly variable interstellar extinction that obscures intrinsic stellar properties and impedes accurate stellar mass determinations.
AI.method: Red clump stars belonging to the Nuclear Bulge were kinematically selected to determine the extinction law. A high-spatial resolution reddening map was created, and stellar mass was computed using completeness-corrected red clump star counts scaled from empirical measurements.
AI.result: A total-to-selective extinction ratio A_K/E_{H-K} = 1.259 ± 0.074 and an extinction ratio A_H/A_K = 1.794 ± 0.046 were found. The reddening map reveals filamentary structures and a gradient over G0.253+0.016 (the Brick). Stellar mass of the Nuclear Bulge is 12.2 ± 2.6 × 10⁸ M☉.
AI.conclusion: The extinction law measurements are consistent with previous works, and the stellar mass estimate agrees with other mass estimates, demonstrating the effectiveness of using kinematically selected red clump stars to overcome extinction challenges.

title: Ultra-deep imaging of nearby dwarf irregular galaxies: stellar haloes and disk structure
summary: We have examined the stellar structure of 10 nearby, low stellar mass (10^6 to 6 x 10^7 Msolar) dwarf irregular galaxies by fitting ellipses as a function of surface brightness on ultra-deep V images. These are compared to far ultraviolet images as tracers of the star formation. We find that the often asymmetrical distribution of large patches of star formation activity in dwarfs, even out to low disk surface brightness levels, skews the broad-band optical isophotes in these galaxies. We also looked for evidence of the presence of a stellar halo. Possible hints of such are found in several galaxies from irregularities in the ellipses, but a stack of seven of the galaxies shows a pure exponential out to a V surface brightness of 32.3 mag/arcsec^2 where the stellar surface density is 0.0013 +/- 0.0011 Msolar/pc^2. The extended stellar component, most likely a disk structure, is probably due to internal evolutionary processes rather than external accretion. The UBVI colors of the annuli are consistent with ages of 1-6 Gyr for the far outer stellar disk.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes 10 nearby dwarf irregular galaxies using ultra-deep V-band images, finding that asymmetrical star formation skews optical isophotes and that the extended stellar component (likely a disk) shows a pure exponential profile down to very low surface brightness, with colors indicating ages of 1-6 Gyr, suggesting internal evolutionary origins rather than external accretion.
AI.motivation: To investigate the stellar structure of low-mass dwarf irregular galaxies and search for evidence of stellar halos, using ultra-deep optical imaging combined with far-UV tracers of star formation.
AI.method: Ellipse fitting as a function of surface brightness on ultra-deep V-band images of 10 nearby dwarf irregular galaxies (M = 10^6 - 6×10^7 M☉), compared with far-UV images tracing star formation. Stacking analysis of 7 galaxies was also performed.
AI.result: Asymmetrical star formation skews broad-band optical isophotes. Stacked image shows a pure exponential profile out to V = 32.3 mag/arcsec² (stellar surface density 0.0013±0.0011 M☉/pc²). UBVI colors of outer annuli are consistent with ages of 1-6 Gyr.
AI.conclusion: The extended stellar component is most likely a disk structure resulting from internal evolutionary processes rather than external accretion. Possible hints of a stellar halo exist in some galaxies but are not robustly confirmed.

title: A Universal Dance of Galactic Disks: Ubiquitous Precession and Its Implications
summary: Precession is a very common phenomenon for small-scale astronomical objects. However, the precession of galactic disks, occurring on a scale larger than kilo-parsec, has barely been studied in the literature. Quantifying this precession in observations remains challenging due to the lack of high-resolution dynamical data. Cosmological simulations, where gravitational interactions are self-consistently modeled, offer a unique avenue for investigating disk precession. Leveraging the IllustrisTNG simulations, we trace the evolution of spin orientation in Milky Way-like galaxies over cosmic time. We find that disk precession is ubiquitous in galaxies and significantly affects galaxy evolution. The precession is driven by the external tidal torque originating from the anisotropic matter distribution within $30\ \mathrm{kpc}$, and is violent at $\mathrm{z} > 1$ and becomes gentler but significant at $\mathrm{z} \sim 0$, when the disks are considered dynamically settled. Disk precession can induce significant cold gas warp, which is often observed in the Milky Way and nearby galaxies. We predict that the Milky Way is precessing at a rate of $\simeq3-10$ degrees per billion years at current epoch based on its observed warp. Violent precession can heat the orbits of stars, which may eventually produce prolate elliptical galaxies. The tidal torque from central galaxies can cause the precession of nearby satellite galaxies and causes their disks to point towards the centrals, which explains the observational radial alignment. We also find that the precession of accreted cold gas stream, regulated by the galaxies' torque, is crucial for the evolution of disk galaxies.

AI.tldr: Using IllustrisTNG simulations, this paper demonstrates that galactic disk precession is ubiquitous in Milky Way-like galaxies, driven by external tidal torques from anisotropic matter within 30 kpc. It affects galaxy evolution through cold gas warping, stellar heating, satellite alignment, and gas stream dynamics, with the Milky Way predicted to precess at 3-10 deg/Gyr.
AI.motivation: Disk precession on kilo-parsec scales has barely been studied observationally due to the lack of high-resolution dynamical data; this work aims to quantify it using cosmological simulations.
AI.method: The study leverages the IllustrisTNG cosmological simulations to trace spin orientation evolution of Milky Way-like galaxies over cosmic time, analyzing precession dynamics and its drivers.
AI.result: Disk precession is ubiquitous, driven by external tidal torque from anisotropic matter within 30 kpc; it is violent at z>1 and gentler but significant at z~0. The Milky Way's precession rate is predicted at ~3-10 deg/Gyr based on its observed warp. Precession causes cold gas warps, stellar orbital heating (potentially forming prolate ellipticals), radial alignment of satellite disks, and governs accreted cold gas stream evolution.
AI.conclusion: Disk precession is a fundamental, ubiquitous process in galaxy evolution that significantly impacts dynamical and structural properties from high redshift to the present epoch.

title: Self-consistent numerical simulations for the formation and dynamics of solar prominences
comment: Includes Main Text, Extended Data and Supplementary Information. Published in Nature Astronomy
summary: Solar prominences are cool and dense plasma structures floating in the hot solar corona. They are ubiquitous features in the solar atmosphere, but their formation mechanism is still unclear. Here we perform comprehensive fully three-dimensional numerical simulations of prominence formation including the physics necessary to describe all atmospheric layers of the sun. With appropriate initial conditions for the magnetic field, solar prominences form self-consistently in the simulations. The formation starts by the random ejection of a dense plasma seed from the chromosphere into the corona. Subsequently, the prominence is built up by a combination of plasma injections from the chromosphere and condensation of inflowing coronal plasma. The prominence properties qualitatively match those of observed prominences. Our findings demonstrate the importance of the dynamics at and below the solar surface in the formation and evolution of solar prominences. This suggests that subsurface dynamics should also be considered in the study of prominence eruptions, which can be associated with coronal mass ejections.

AI.tldr: Using 3D numerical simulations including all solar atmospheric layers, the study demonstrates that solar prominences form self-consistently through chromospheric plasma injections and coronal plasma condensation, highlighting the critical role of subsurface dynamics in prominence formation and evolution.
AI.motivation: Solar prominences are ubiquitous but their formation mechanism remains unclear. Understanding this process is important because prominence eruptions can trigger coronal mass ejections that affect space weather.
AI.method: Comprehensive fully three-dimensional numerical simulations incorporating physics necessary to describe all atmospheric layers of the Sun, with appropriate initial magnetic field conditions.
AI.result: Prominences form self-consistently through a two-stage process: (1) random ejection of dense plasma seeds from the chromosphere into the corona, followed by (2) a combination of plasma injections from the chromosphere and condensation of inflowing coronal plasma. The simulated prominences qualitatively match observed prominence properties.
AI.conclusion: Dynamics at and below the solar surface are crucial for prominence formation and evolution, suggesting subsurface dynamics should also be considered when studying prominence eruptions and associated coronal mass ejections.

title: XMAGNET -- Stir before serving: a Lagrangian perspective on mixing-driven condensation in the intracluster medium
comment: 15 pages, 16 figures, submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics, comments welcome!
summary: We aim to characterize the thermodynamic and dynamical conditions leading to condensation in cluster cores, and to assess the role of magnetic fields. We implement a Monte-Carlo tracer particle algorithm in the GPU-accelerated code AthenaPK, and run a purely hydrodynamical and a magnetohydrodynamical (MHD) simulations of an idealized cool-core cluster. We identify the subset of hot ICM tracers that undergo a transition to the cold phase and reconstruct their histories over a lookback time of $300\,\mathrm{Myr}$ prior to condensation. In both runs, the large majority of tracers transitioning to the cold phase follow a thermodynamic pathway driven by mixing, whereby hot ambient gas is entrained onto low-entropy seed clumps that subsequently grow into larger clouds and filaments. In the hydrodynamical run, these seeds form mainly via in-situ cooling at the edges of AGN cavities. In the MHD run, the cold gas cycle is more complex: AGN outflows occasionally shred portions of existing filaments into fragments which are then uplifted, seeding further condensation. In the MHD run, the properties of condensing tracers begin to diverge from the background ICM significantly earlier than in the hydrodynamical run (${\sim}150\,\rm Myr$ before the cooling transition versus ${\sim}30\,\rm Myr$), with vorticity and magnetic energy growing together. The turbulent Mach number at condensation is also systematically lower than in the hydrodynamical run. We examine the post-condensation evolution of individual cold structures in the MHD run, namely a massive core filament and two isolated clouds in quiescent regions. We find that magnetic tension dominates over ram pressure as the primary drag force, significantly reducing the clouds' terminal velocity. Our results demonstrate that magnetic fields substantially impact the assembly history and kinematic properties of the cold phase in cool-core clusters.

AI.tldr: This paper uses Monte-Carlo tracer particles in hydro and MHD simulations of a cool-core cluster to study how magnetic fields affect the condensation of cold gas from the hot ICM. Mixing-driven condensation dominates in both runs, but MHD alters the cold gas cycle, extends precursor timescales, and increases magnetic drag on cold clouds.
AI.motivation: To characterize the thermodynamic and dynamical conditions leading to condensation in cluster cores, and to assess the role of magnetic fields in this process.
AI.method: Monte-Carlo tracer particle algorithm implemented in the GPU-accelerated code AthenaPK; purely hydrodynamical and MHD simulations of an idealized cool-core cluster; reconstruction of tracer histories over 300 Myr prior to condensation.
AI.result: Condensation is driven by mixing in both runs, with low-entropy seed clumps growing via entrainment. In hydro, seeds form via in-situ cooling at AGN cavity edges; in MHD, AGN outflows shred existing filaments into fragments that seed further condensation. In MHD, tracers diverge from background ICM ~150 Myr before cooling (vs. ~30 Myr in hydro), with correlated vorticity and magnetic energy growth. MHD clouds have lower turbulent Mach numbers. Magnetic tension dominates over ram pressure as the primary drag force on cold clouds, reducing their terminal velocity.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic fields substantially impact the assembly history and kinematic properties of the cold phase in cool-core clusters, affecting both the condensation pathway and the dynamics of the resulting cold gas structures.

title: EMBER: Machine-Learning Detection of Modulated Ion Acoustic Waves and Associated Core-Electron Heating in the Solar Wind with Parker Solar Probe
summary: Modulated ion acoustic waves (IAWs) -- including triggered ion acoustic waves (TIAWs) and frequency-dispersed ion acoustic waves (FDIAWs) -- are increasingly recognized as efficient drivers of electron heating in the solar wind through nonlinear wave-particle interactions. Identification of these events in the Parker Solar Probe (PSP) FIELDS burst-mode archive has so far relied on expert visual inspection and does not scale to the full mission. We present EMBER (Electron heating from Modulated Burst-mode Event Recognition), an open-source pipeline that converts PSP FIELDS Digital Burst Memory (DBM) voltage bursts into log-scaled Fourier spectrograms and applies a multi-detector, background-only anomaly detection suite. The suite combines physics-motivated detectors, classical outlier detectors, and deep learning detectors. The EMBER ensemble recovers 93% of the anomalous events at 1% FAR (1 false positive per 100 held-out backgrounds). Coincident SWEAP/SPAN diagnostics show that flagged intervals exhibit core perpendicular electron temperatures above the adiabatic cooling expectation and elevated Te/Ti, reproducing the preferential-heating phenomenology established by prior manual studies without any use of electron temperatures in the detection step.

AI.tldr: EMBER is an open-source pipeline that uses a multi-detector anomaly detection suite (physics-motivated, classical, and deep learning detectors) to automatically identify modulated ion acoustic waves in PSP FIELDS burst-mode data, recovering 93% of anomalous events at 1% FAR and reproducing electron heating signatures without using temperature information.
AI.motivation: Identification of modulated IAWs (TIAWs and FDIAWs) in PSP FIELDS burst-mode data has relied on expert visual inspection, which does not scale to the full mission. An automated, scalable detection method is needed.
AI.method: The EMBER pipeline converts PSP FIELDS DBM voltage bursts into log-scaled Fourier spectrograms and applies a multi-detector ensemble combining physics-motivated detectors, classical outlier detectors, and deep learning detectors for background-only anomaly detection.
AI.result: The ensemble recovers 93% of anomalous events at 1% FAR. Coincident SWEAP/SPAN diagnostics show flagged intervals exhibit core perpendicular electron temperatures above adiabatic cooling expectation and elevated Te/Ti, reproducing preferential-heating phenomenology without using electron temperatures in detection.
AI.conclusion: EMBER enables scalable, automated detection of modulated IAWs in PSP data and successfully identifies intervals with electron heating signatures consistent with prior manual studies, demonstrating that temperature information is not required for detection.

title: Exploring RR Lyrae Variable Stars in the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Data Preview 1
comment: 14 pages, 11 figures and 2 tables. AJ accepted
summary: We investigate the properties of known RR Lyrae in the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Data Preview 1 (DP1) fields and compare those with the predictions based on stellar pulsation models tailored to the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) filters. The cross-match of the DP1 data with two public variable star catalogs resulted in $\sim 600$ RR Lyrae with adequate light curve sampling in five (out of seven) DP1 fields. The majority of RR Lyrae are in the 47 Tucanae and Fornax fields. We estimated photometric metallicities for these RR Lyrae using the theoretical metallicity-color relation based on $gri$-band data, and find a good agreement with literature values where the light curve sampling is sufficient for fitting template light curves accurately. The distance modulus to all RR Lyrae in DP1 fields were determined using the theoretical period-luminosity-metallicity (PLZ) relations and the $W_{gr}$ period-Wesenheit-metallicity (PWZ) relation which has the smallest metallicity term. The distances based on PWZ relations are in good agreement with the literature values with a mean offset of $0.01\pm0.36$~mag. However, the PLZ-based distance moduli are systematically large which could be due to the theoretical calibration uncertainties that include evolved horizontal branch models. The predicted period-amplitude relations based on evolved models are also inconsistent with the amplitudes based on DP1 light curves. We conclude that the metallicity and distance estimates are sensitive to the template fitting to sparsely sampled light curves in DP1 data and future data release will significantly improve these determinations for RR Lyrae stars.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes ~600 RR Lyrae stars in Rubin Observatory DP1 fields, validating theoretical metallicity-color and period-luminosity-metallicity relations against observations in LSST filters. PWZ-based distances agree well with literature (offset 0.01±0.36 mag), but PLZ distances are systematically biased, possibly due to evolved horizontal branch model uncertainties. Period-amplitude relations from evolved models also disagree with DP1 data. Sparse light curve sampling limits accuracy, expected to improve with future data releases.
AI.motivation: To validate theoretical stellar pulsation models (metallicity-color, PLZ, PWZ relations) for RR Lyrae stars using the first Rubin Observatory LSST data (DP1), and assess how well these models perform with sparsely sampled light curves in LSST filters.
AI.method: Cross-matched DP1 data with two public variable star catalogs, yielding ~600 RR Lyrae in five DP1 fields. Estimated photometric metallicities via theoretical gri-band metallicity-color relations. Determined distance moduli using PLZ and PWZ relations. Compared predicted period-amplitude relations from evolved models against DP1 light curve amplitudes.
AI.result: PWZ-based distances match literature values well (mean offset 0.01±0.36 mag). PLZ-based distances are systematically too large. Period-amplitude relations from evolved models are inconsistent with DP1 observations. Metallicity and distance estimates are sensitive to template fitting quality given sparse light curve sampling.
AI.conclusion: Metallicity and distance estimates for RR Lyrae in DP1 are limited by sparse light curve sampling; future data releases will significantly improve accuracy. Evolved horizontal branch models may need revision to better match LSST observations.

title: Kinematic properties of the TW Hya association
summary: A kinematic analysis of the young stellar association TWHya has been performed. The components of the displacement matrix in the Ogorodnikov-Milne linear model have been estimated both graphically and by solving the basic kinematic equations. The association's volume expansion with a coefficient of $K_{xyz}=103\pm9$ km s$^{-1}$ kpc$^{-1}$ was confirmed, which yields a dynamical age estimate of $t=9.7 \pm0.8$ Myr. Using the graphical method, estimates of the association's proper rigid-body rotation parameters $ω$ around the galactic axes x and y have been obtained for the first time, with velocity values in the range of 50-70 km s$^{-1}$ kpc$^{-1}$ and errors in their determination of 14-19 km s$^{-1}$ kpc$^{-1}$. However, these values are not confirmed by another method. For example, when solving kinematic equations only using proper motions, all three components of rigid body rotation do not differ significantly from zero, $(ω_x,ω_y,ω_z)=(4,7,11)\pm(5,5,5)$ km s$^{-1}$ kpc$^{-1}$.

AI.tldr: A kinematic analysis of the TW Hydrae association using the Ogorodnikov-Milne model confirms its expansion (K_xyz=103±9 km/s/kpc, dynamical age 9.7±0.8 Myr) but yields conflicting results for rigid-body rotation: graphical method suggests ω_x,ω_y ~50-70 km/s/kpc, while solving proper-motion equations finds all three rotation components consistent with zero.
AI.motivation: To kinematically characterize the young stellar association TW Hydrae, including its expansion and rotation, to better understand its dynamical state and age.
AI.method: Application of the Ogorodnikov-Milne linear model via (1) graphical estimation and (2) solving basic kinematic equations using proper motions only.
AI.result: Confirmed volume expansion K_xyz=103±9 km/s/kpc with dynamical age 9.7±0.8 Myr. Graphical method yields ω_x, ω_y ~50-70 km/s/kpc (errors 14-19); however, proper-motion-only solutions give (ω_x,ω_y,ω_z)=(4,7,11)±(5,5,5) km/s/kpc, all consistent with zero.
AI.conclusion: The association is expanding, but evidence for rigid-body rotation is method-dependent and inconclusive; the graphical rotation estimates are not corroborated by the kinematic equation approach.

title: Magnetic loops in the solar transition region
comment: An invited review to appear on RMPP, 32 pages
summary: Transition region (TR) loops are arcade-like features in the solar transition region, with temperatures roughly between $2\times10^4$ K and $6\times10^5$ K. They are a fundamental building block of TR, which are results of the coupling between the magnetic field and the TR plasma. Their dynamics is closely related to the transport of energy and mass through the TR. Studies on this class of loops since the launch of the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS) have revealed that they are distinct from coronal loops. Observations have revealed that they are associated with many small-scale dynamic phenomena in the TR, from which one can infer the physics behind the energy and mass transfer in a magnetically confined environment at TR temperature. This review summarises the observational results of TR loops, showing their morphology, dynamics, plasma parameters, their relationship with flux emergence, their heating properties, and their implication in the heating of the solar atmosphere. This class of magnetic loops is much less well understood than their coronal counterparts. This review also concludes with several critical questions that need to be answered in the coming era with more advanced observational techniques and more precise and realistic simulations.

AI.tldr: This review summarizes observational results on solar transition region (TR) loops (2×10⁴ K to 6×10⁵ K), highlighting their morphology, dynamics, plasma parameters, relationship with flux emergence, heating properties, and role in solar atmosphere heating, while noting they are less understood than coronal loops and outlining key open questions.
AI.motivation: TR loops are a fundamental building block of the transition region, intimately tied to magnetic field-plasma coupling and energy/mass transport. They are distinct from coronal loops and associated with many small-scale dynamic phenomena, making them crucial for understanding energy and mass transfer in magnetically confined TR environments.
AI.method: The paper is a review that synthesizes observational results of TR loops, primarily leveraging data from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS) to characterize their morphology, dynamics, plasma parameters, flux emergence relationships, and heating properties.
AI.result: Observations since IRIS reveal TR loops are distinct from coronal loops; they exhibit small-scale dynamic phenomena that provide insights into energy and mass transfer in magnetically confined environments at TR temperatures. Their morphology, dynamics, plasma properties, and heating behavior have been characterized, and their relationship with flux emergence is established.
AI.conclusion: TR loops are much less understood than coronal loops. Critical open questions remain that will require more advanced observational techniques and more precise, realistic simulations to answer in the coming era.

title: A Global 7% Systemic Sensitivity Floor in Gaia DR3: Multi-Wavelength Validation using 2MASS, Pan-STARRS and the 0.75-Magnitude Offset
summary:
This study performs a multi-wavelength astrometric and photometric examination of a high-confidence sample $(N = 120,418)$ derived from a parent population of 2.36 million unique WDSS-seeded systems. By establishing an empirical polynomial ridge line for the broader Gaia-2MASS-Pan-STARRS subset, we calculated magnitude residuals $(ΔG)$ to probe the systemic limits of the Gaia single-star model. Results reveal a distinct "Detection Gap" manifested as a tri-modal distribution: 14,705 stars $(12\%)$ were identified as overt Astrometric Discordance failures $(\mathrm{RUWE} > 1.4)$, while a significant subset of candidates exhibits signs of Astrometric Suppression -- where dual-flux profiles are absorbed into a stable single-star solution $(\mathrm{RUWE} < 1.4)$ despite the physical presence of a companion.
  Crucially, while the raw failure rate reaches $12\%$ globally, we identify an asymptotic Intrinsic Binary Residual (IBR) of $\approx 7.0\%$ $(\approx 8,429$ sources) that persists independently of stellar density. Utilizing a "Triple Constraint" framework -- astrometric noise (RUWE), photometric excess $(ΔG)$, and the absence of official Non-Single Star (NSS) classification -- we identify a $5.9\%$ Detection Gap subset within the Gaia-2MASS audit chain that is consistent with a population of "orphaned" binaries clustered near the theoretical -0.75 magnitude "Binary Ridge." This $7\%$ floor is interpreted here as an apparent global sensitivity limit in the Gaia pipeline, suggesting that local stellar mass density models -- which rely on single-star mass-to-light ratios -- may require a quantifiable correction to accurately reflect the local baryonic mass budget.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes 120,418 high-confidence multi-wavelength systems from a parent sample of 2.36 million WDSS-seeded sources, revealing a tri-modal "Detection Gap" where 12% show overt astrometric failures (RUWE>1.4) and additional sources exhibit Astrometric Suppression. An Intrinsic Binary Residual (IBR) of ≈7.0% is identified as a persistent global sensitivity floor in Gaia, suggesting that single-star mass models require quantifiable corrections for missing binary contributions.
AI.motivation: To quantify the limits of Gaia's single-star model by identifying unresolved binary systems that evade detection through astrometric and photometric diagnostics, and to assess the impact of undetected binaries on local baryonic mass budget estimates.
AI.method: Multi-wavelength astrometric and photometric analysis of 120,418 high-confidence systems from 2.36 million WDSS-seeded sources; empirical polynomial ridge line fitting for Gaia-2MASS-Pan-STARRS subset; calculation of magnitude residuals (ΔG); Triple Constraint framework combining RUWE, ΔG, and absence of NSS classification.
AI.result: Tri-modal Detection Gap distribution: 12% overt RUWE failures; Astrometric Suppression cases (RUWE<1.4 despite companions); asymptotic Intrinsic Binary Residual of ≈7.0% (8,429 sources) independent of stellar density; 5.9% subset of "orphaned" binaries near the -0.75 mag Binary Ridge.
AI.conclusion: Gaia's pipeline has a ~7% global sensitivity limit for detecting binary systems, implying that local stellar mass density models relying on single-star mass-to-light ratios need a quantifiable correction to accurately reflect the true baryonic mass budget.

title: PEARLS: Two Distinct Populations of AGN Hosts Moving Between Star Formation and Quiescence
summary: We present the results of AGN--host-galaxy decomposition using JWST/NIRCam, HST/ACS, and HST/WFC3 imaging of the North Ecliptic Pole Time Domain Field (NEP-TDF). The light-profiles of 36 NIRCam-selected AGN candidates are modeled for measurement of their point sources, and point source-subtracted host-galaxy emission is used in SED modeling for star formation rate (SFR) estimation. Offsets from the canonical star-forming main sequence (SFMS) show that the host galaxies form two distinct groups distinguished by their star formation: a ``bridge'' between the moderate SFRs of radio sources and low SFRs of X-ray sources, and a cleanly-separated ``branch'' above $Δ\rm SFMS = -1$ whose SFR trends positively with AGN fraction. Branch galaxies include late-type galaxies with X-ray and radio detections and more dominant point sources that are most certainly AGN, while bridge galaxies have predominantly early-type morphologies with weaker point sources that may be due to compact stellar bulges. Both groups show evidence of recent transition between star formation and quiescence, but neither group shows preference for higher or lower stellar mass or redshift, suggesting that star formation in NIRCam-selected AGN-hosts is more strongly determined by AGN activity than by stellar mass.

AI.tldr: AGN-host galaxy decomposition using JWST, HST, and NIRCam imaging of the NEP-TDF reveals two distinct groups of host galaxies: a "bridge" (low SFR, early-type, radio/X-ray) and a "branch" (higher SFR, late-type, stronger AGN point sources), with star formation more dependent on AGN activity than stellar mass.
AI.motivation: To characterize the star formation properties of AGN host galaxies and understand the relationship between AGN activity and host-galaxy star formation using high-resolution multi-wavelength imaging.
AI.method: JWST/NIRCam, HST/ACS, and HST/WFC3 imaging of 36 NIRCam-selected AGN candidates in the NEP-TDF; light-profile decomposition to separate point sources from host galaxies; SED modeling of host-galaxy emission for SFR estimation; comparison to the canonical star-forming main sequence.
AI.result: Two distinct host-galaxy groups: a "bridge" with moderate-to-low SFRs (radio to X-ray sources) and a "branch" above ΔSFMS = -1 with positive SFR-AGN fraction trends. Branch galaxies are late-type with strong AGN point sources; bridge galaxies are early-type with weaker point sources possibly from compact bulges.
AI.conclusion: Star formation in NIRCam-selected AGN hosts is more strongly determined by AGN activity than by stellar mass or redshift, with both groups showing evidence of recent star formation-quiescence transition.
